content.content: Legazpi's fleet arrives in Samar, anchoring in Gamay Bay (historically recorded as Cibaobao). Legazpi sends two boats to find a safe harbor; Spanish officer Francisco Gomez ventures ashore alone and is immediately killed by native warriors on the beach.

Legazpi's fleet enters Cebu's harbor. Rajah Tupas refuses three peace embassies; Spanish ship artillery bombards the native proas, and a stray shell sets fire to a nipa hut, burning down over a hundred native homes as villagers retreat to the hills.

Seaman Juan de Camus discovers a Flemish-style image of the Child Jesus (the Santo Niño) in an unburned hut — originally gifted by Antonio Pigafetta to the Queen of Cebu during Magellan's 1521 expedition. The relic features a red wooden cap and gilded tin collar.
Fort San Pedro is built; Legazpi establishes the first permanent Spanish settlement, first named Villa de San Miguel, later renamed Villa de Santísimo Nombre de Jesús.
A period of severe famine; the garrison survives on grass, palm leaves, rats, and mice.

sub-content.content: French pilot Pierre Plin and Spanish soldier Pablo Hernandez plot to steal the vessel San Juan; they're captured and hanged by Martín de Goiti, with Hernandez's head placed on a fort stake.
The supply vessel San Jerónimo arrives but does little to relieve the famine.

content.content: To escape famine and a third Portuguese blockade under Gonzalo Pereira, Legazpi relocates the colony to the Panay River — described by Augustinian friars as hot, marshy, and prone to flooding.
Martín de Goiti and Juan de Salcedo depart Panay for Luzon with two ships (the San Miguel and the Tortuga) and fifteen native proas.

King Philip II names the archipelago the Kingdom of New Castile and decrees Manila its capital. Legazpi establishes Manila's first municipal government (cabildo), appointing two mayors and twelve aldermen. The indigenous rulers associated with Lakandula and Soliman accept vassalage, submitting to Spanish authority.

Francisco Dagohoy leads 3,000 Inabangans and Talibonese to the mountains of Bohol. The rebellion is sparked when Father Gaspar Morales refuses a Christian burial for Dagohoy's brother, Sagarino. In retaliation, the rebels kill Jesuit priest Father Giuseppe Lamberti (January 24, 1744) and later execute Morales.

The rebels built a self-sufficient mountain settlement in the Inabanga and Cayelanga Mountains, growing to 20,000 followers by 1770. They repel Cebu's Bishop Miguel Lino de Espeleta and twenty separate Spanish military campaigns.
A Spanish expedition of 2,200 native and Spanish troops fails to reach the mountain strongholds.

The 85-year rebellion ends after a year-long campaign (begun 1825) by 6,000 native troops under Captain Manuel Sanz, ordered by Governor-General Mariano Ricafort. Ricafort pardons 19,420 survivors, who resettle in Batuanan, Cabulao, Catigbian, and Bilar.
Dr. José Rizal returns to Manila from Hong Kong, having concluded that reform had to be pursued directly in the homeland.
Rizal formally establishes La Liga Filipina at Doroteo Ongjunco's Tondo home; the founding assembly includes Bonifacio and Arellano.
Governor-General Eulogio Despujol orders Rizal's arrest and detention at Fort Santiago.

Despujol decrees Rizal's exile to Dapitan. That evening, a secret council — Bonifacio, Arellano, Diaz, Diwa, Dizon, and Plata — gathers at Arellano's house on Calle Elcano, Tondo, and formally founds the Katipunan (KKK).
Bonifacio and Jacinto redefine 'Tagalog' to mean anyone born in the archipelago, conceiving the sovereign nation of Katagalugan.
Deodato Arellano was chosen as the first president of the Katipunan's Supreme Council; that same month, the slow Sistemang Patatsulok (Triangle System) was set aside in favor of open recruitment.
La Liga Filipina is revived; Domingo Franco is elected president, Arellano is secretary-treasurer, and Bonifacio is chief of propaganda.
Ideological splits prove irreconcilable; the Liga formally dissolves. Conservatives form the Cuerpo de Compromisarios; radicals commit fully to the Katipunan.
Emilio Jacinto joins the Katipunan (1894) and drafts the Kartilya ng Katipunan, a primer of fourteen moral and civic guideposts. Bonifacio adopts it as the official guide, replacing his own Dekalogo.
As Spanish surveillance intensifies, Gregoria de Jesús safeguards the Katipunan's documents, seals, and revolvers, frequently relocating them.
The Katipunan publishes the sole issue of Kalayaan, falsely datelined 'Yokohama'; membership grows to an estimated 30,000.

Katipunan member Teodoro Patiño confesses the society's existence to his sister Honoria at a Mandaluyong orphanage; at the urging of Sor Teresa de Jesús, Father Mariano Gil is alerted and raids the Diario de Manila press. Spanish authorities launch raids and mass arrests.
Bonifacio and thousands of Katipuneros gather at the outskirts of Manila and tear up their cédulas personales — the Cry of Pugad Lawin (also called the Cry of Balintawak).

Bonifacio convenes the Kataastaasang Kapulungan (National Assembly) in Melchora Aquino's barn in Kalookan. The leaders declare a nationwide armed revolution, establish an open de facto national government, and elect the movement's supreme officials.
Bonifacio and his generals schedule a coordinated midnight assault on Manila.

The assault on Manila fails; the rebels, outmatched, shift to attack-and-withdraw operations. Governor-General Ramón Blanco declares a state of war across eight provinces: Manila, Bulacan, Pampanga, Nueva Ecija, Tarlac, Laguna, Cavite, and Batangas, launching mass arrests and reprisals.
The Katipuneros attack the Spanish weapons depot and garrison at San Juan del Monte.

KKK lodges across Cavite seize local governments; Magdalo forces under Aguinaldo win rapid victories. Success widens a rift, splitting the rebels into the Magdiwang (loyal to Bonifacio) and Magdalo (under Aguinaldo) councils.
Dr. José Rizal is executed by firing squad at Bagumbayan, approved by Governor-General Camilo de Polavieja — a defining, sorrowful moment that unifies national consciousness.
Domingo Franco and Jose Dizon are executed by firing squad at Bagumbayan, honored as two of the Thirteen Martyrs of Bagumbayan.
Teodoro Plata is executed by firing squad at Bagumbayan.
Bonifacio travels to Cavite to mediate the Magdiwang–Magdalo rivalry; deep divisions persist.

The Tejeros Convention convenes in Cavite; Aguinaldo is elected President in absentia, Bonifacio is elected Director of the Interior. Magdalo delegate Daniel Tirona publicly challenges Bonifacio's qualifications; Bonifacio, insulted and ignored, dissolves the assembly and declares the results null and void.
Bonifacio convenes a second assembly to formally document his objection. Aguinaldo, Mariano Trías, and Artemio Ricarte take their oaths of office at the Tanza convent.
Bonifacio and his loyalists withdrew to Naik, refusing to recognize Aguinaldo's government (the Naik Agreement).

A confrontation at Limbon, Indang, Cavite: Aguinaldo's troops assault Bonifacio's camp. Ciriaco Bonifacio is killed; Andrés is wounded and captured with his brother Procopio and wife Gregoria de Jesús.

A court-martial under General Mariano Noriel convicts the Bonifacio brothers of treason and sedition. Aguinaldo's initial order commuting the sentence to banishment was withdrawn under pressure from his generals.
Andrés and Procopio Bonifacio are executed by firing squad at Mount Buntig, Maragondon.
The Pact of Biak-na-Bato is signed: Spain pays indemnity, and Aguinaldo and his cabinet go into voluntary exile in Hong Kong.

The Spanish-American War begins after the sinking of the USS Maine. U.S. consuls E. Spencer Pratt (Singapore) and Rounsevelle Wildman (Hong Kong) meet Aguinaldo, encouraging his return and assuring him the U.S. has no colonial ambitions.
Admiral George Dewey defeats the Spanish fleet in Manila Bay.
Aguinaldo returns to the Philippines aboard the USS McCulloch; meets Dewey aboard the USS Olympia, who advises that raising a national flag will lend the cause credibility.
Aguinaldo establishes a Dictatorial Government to manage the rapid capture of the provinces.
The Battle of Alapan: over 270 Spanish naval infantry surrender. The Hong Kong-sewn Philippine flag is unfurled for the first time at the Teatro Caviteño, Cavite City.
Aguinaldo formally declares Philippine independence from his residence in Kawit, Cavite, before a massive crowd.
Guided by Apolinario Mabini, Aguinaldo decrees the transition from the Dictatorial Government to a structured Revolutionary Government.
Spain and the U.S. stage a 'mock battle' for Manila; Filipino forces are barred from the assault and excluded from the surrender negotiations.
The Treaty of Paris is signed: Spain cedes the Philippines, Guam, and Puerto Rico to the U.S. for $20 million, without Filipino representation.
President William McKinley issues the Benevolent Assimilation Proclamation, declaring U.S. sovereignty over the Philippines before the Senate has even ratified the Treaty of Paris.
McKinley creates the First Philippine Commission (Schurman Commission), which concludes Filipinos 'are not ready for self-rule'.
American sentries fatally shoot a Filipino army corporal at the Santa Mesa Bridge, Manila, triggering retaliatory gunfire and a U.S. offensive — the start of the Philippine-American War.

tiers.content: Chief of Cebu.
Protected his people by evacuating them to the hills and launching a passive starvation blockade rather than accepting vassalage immediately.
Legazpi's Master-of-Camp; led pacification and foraging expeditions in Cebu, Panay, Negros and Leyte.
Led the May 3, 1570 expedition to Luzon; captured Maynila and burned fifteen hundred homes.
Legazpi's 21-year-old grandson; won native sympathy through valor and diplomacy.
At 23 led a four-month pacification campaign around northern Luzon, Pangasinan and the eastern coasts.
In his will he named the native Filipinos of his Vigan encomienda heirs to most of his estate.
Boholano cabeza de barangay; his brother Sagarino has died.
Also called Francisco Sendrijas; used guerrilla skill and charisma to lead followers away from exploitation, unfair taxes and forced labor.
Mobilized up to 20,000 followers deep in the Bohol mountains.
Led the longest rebellion in Philippine history, 1744-1829.
Jesuit parish priest of Inabanga, Bohol.
His refusal to bury Dagohoy's brother, who died on Morales's own orders while pursuing a fugitive, was the immediate catalyst for the rebellion.
Later captured and executed by Dagohoy's forces.
Spanish officer sent to retake Bohol.
Landed in April 1828 and spent over a year with 6,000 native troops subduing the mountain strongholds.
Governor-General of the Philippines, 1825-1830, tasked with reclaiming Bohol.
Paired prolonged campaigns with amnesty; pardoned and resettled 19,420 survivors instead of fighting on.
Author of Noli Me Tángere and El Filibusterismo, whose exposure of clerical corruption inspired national consciousness.
Founder of La Liga Filipina; influenced by Rousseau's social contract; believed Filipinos must build collective civic virtue to earn independence.
Arrested and exiled to Dapitan in 1892.
Declined Bonifacio's invitation to join the Katipunan.
Implicated in the 1896 uprising; executed December 30, 1896; remembered every year as Rizal Day.
Born to a working-class family in Tondo, November 30, 1863; self-taught.
Founding member of La Liga Filipina; convinced by Rizal's exile that peaceful petitioning was futile; co-founded the Katipunan the same evening Rizal was exiled.
Unified the movement under the inclusive Tagalog nation, Katagalugan.
Organized the Katipunan's first national cabinet and directed its first attacks; set up guerrilla networks north of the Pasig; known as president of the Tagalog Republic.
Traveled to Cavite to mediate the Magdiwang-Magdalo rivalry.
Annulled the Tejeros elections and withdrew to Naik, refusing to recognize Aguinaldo's government.
Arrested at Limbon and court-martialed for treason; executed May 10, 1897; honored as a foremost national hero on Bonifacio Day.
Brilliant, self-taught lawyer and writer, son of an unlettered farmer; paralyzed by polio.
Launched his career in the 1893 Liga revival as Supreme Council secretary; founded the Junta de Compromisarios to keep funding La Solidaridad; Grand Orator in December 1893.

Became Aguinaldo's chief adviser in 1898 and pushed the shift to a constitutional Revolutionary Government; first cabinet president; 'brains of the First Philippine Republic'; wrote El Verdadero Decálogo; saw the revolution as part of a Pan-Malay emancipation.
Refused allegiance to the United States; exiled to Guam in 1901 with Ricarte; relented in 1903 due to failing health.
Reformist clerk at the Spanish military arsenal; married to Hilaria, sister of Marcelo H. del Pilar.
Founding secretary of La Liga Filipina; first president of the Katipunan's Supreme Council, October 1892.
Governor-General who ordered Rizal's arrest at Fort Santiago on July 6, 1892 on trumped-up charges.
Ordered the exile the next day, directly catalyzing the founding of the Katipunan that evening.
Reformist lawyer and merchant, born in Mambusao, Capiz, August 4, 1856.
Studied law at UST; friend of Mabini; fellow member of Logia Balagtas No. 149; entrusted with the Liga's documents; elected president of the revived Liga, April 3, 1893.
Arrested after the Katipunan was exposed; executed January 11, 1897, one of the Thirteen Martyrs of Bagumbayan.
Founding Katipunan member, born in Paoay, Ilocos Norte; court clerk in Binondo; Liga member.
Masonic name Tupas, Logia Taliba No. 165; served on the Supreme Council, 1892-1893.
Signed the Pact and went to Hong Kong with Aguinaldo; Colonel in the Philippine-American War; died 1916.
Born in San Roque, Cavite; studied at UST with Plata; worked as a court clerk.
Co-founded the Katipunan on July 7, 1892; Masonic name Baguio, Logia Taliba No. 165.
Arrested in Betis, Pampanga after the exposure; freed under the Pact; joined Trías and helped force the García Peña surrender in May 1898; Malolos delegate; died March 12, 1930.
Merchant and Katipunan co-founder; Venerable Master of Logia Taliba No. 165; uncle of Emilio Jacinto.
Rejected the reformist Cuerpo de Compromisarios to join Bonifacio's armed path.
Executed at Bagumbayan on January 11, 1897, one of the Thirteen Martyrs.
Katipunan co-founder; cousin of Gregoria de Jesús; Diwa's friend from UST; husband of Bonifacio's sister Espiridiona.
Secretary of War in Bonifacio's de facto cabinet, August 1896.
Executed by firing squad at Bagumbayan in February 1897.
19-year-old UST law student, nephew of Jose Dizon; Bonifacio's closest adviser; 'Brains of the Katipunan'.
Intellectualized the society's aims; authored the Kartilya ng Katipunan, its moral primer.
Edited the newspaper Kalayaan.
Wife of Bonifacio, cousin of Plata; the Katipunan's Lakambini (Muse).
Counter-intelligence role: kept records, seals and supplies safe by moving them constantly (per some accounts, sleeping on the documents during raids).
Present at Bonifacio's capture at Limbon in 1897.
83-year-old widow who ran a local store.
Hosted the August 24, 1896 national assembly in her barn in Banlat, Kalookan, giving food and sanctuary to the rebels.
Arrested for her support; imprisoned at Bilibid and exiled to the Mariana Islands.
Katipunan member and typesetter at the Diario de Manila press.
On August 19, 1896 he told his sister at the orphanage, giving the confirming leak that exposed the society; later testified before Col. Francisco Olive y García.
Teodoro's sister, raised by Augustinian nuns at a Mandaluyong orphanage; her distress led her to confide in the orphanage director.
Mother Superior of the Mandaluyong orphanage; escorted the Patiño siblings to reveal the conspiracy to the parish priest of Tondo.
Augustinian curate and parish priest of Tondo.
After the Patiño confession he alerted the Guardia Civil and led the August 19 raid on the Diario de Manila press, seizing lithographic stones and membership rosters.
President of the Magdiwang Council in Cavite; previously jailed by Spain for anti-colonial agitation.
Remained fiercely loyal to Bonifacio, resisting Magdalo attempts to bypass the Supreme Council.
Member of Cavite's provincial elite and mayor of Kawit.
Initiated into Masonry in 1895; joined the Katipunan as 'Magdalo'; disciplined strategy and quick victories in Cavite won him the revolutionary forces.
Elected President at Tejeros; dismantled the Katipunan's structures and reorganized the Tagalog Republic into the República Filipina.
Negotiated the Pact of Biak-na-Bato, December 1897.
After exile, declared Philippine independence at Kawit on June 12, 1898, and with Mabini's guidance turned the Dictatorship into a constitutional Revolutionary Government.
Prominent Magdalo leader.
Publicly challenged Bonifacio's qualifications for Director of the Interior, citing his lack of a lawyer's diploma, and shattered the assembly.
The split he set off ended in Bonifacio's arrest and execution.
Prominent general and close associate of Bonifacio; stopped Bonifacio from shooting Tirona during the election.
Took the oath under protest but honestly recorded the convention's irregularities in his memoirs, preserving the record.
Senior revolutionary general who presided over the court-martial and delivered the treason and sedition verdict that led to the executions.
Prominent Caviteño revolutionary leader, active Freemason, general.
In May-June 1898 his forces compelled the surrender of Cavite's Spanish commander, Gen. Leopoldo García Peña.
Appointed Secretary of Finance in Aguinaldo's first Cabinet, January 2, 1899.
Reformist lawyer and legal adviser to Aguinaldo in the revolution's second phase.
Wrote and read the Act of the Declaration of Independence on June 12, 1898.
Commander of the American Asiatic Squadron; destroyed the Spanish Pacific fleet at Manila Bay on May 1, 1898.
Sent the McCulloch to bring Aguinaldo home and advised him aboard the Olympia that a national flag would lend the cause credibility.
U.S. consul-general in Singapore who urged Aguinaldo to return, saying the U.S. had no colonial ambitions and fought only to free Cuba.
Reportedly said Dewey guaranteed U.S. recognition of independence, though nothing was ever signed.
U.S. consul-general in Hong Kong who, with Pratt, gave verbal assurances of support and helped arrange the McCulloch passage.
U.S. President during both wars; focused on domestic recovery and tried to avoid conflict with Spain.

Refused to recognize Philippine independence (Benevolent Assimilation Proclamation, December 21, 1898); created the Schurman Commission on January 21, 1899, which found Filipinos 'not ready for self-rule'.
Assassinated September 6, 1901; succeeded by Theodore Roosevelt.

content.meaning: The head official of a province or judicial district, responsible for provincial administration and tax collection; many holders were criticized for abusing this power for personal gain.

'Sons of the People' / 'Children of the Nation'— the sacred password and identity of first-degree Katipunan members (Katipon), reflecting the society's commitment to human equality and rejection of colonial hierarchy.
A Catholic congregation that administered educational and charitable institutions in the colonial Philippines, including the Mandaluyong Orphanage — the site of the Katipunan's exposure in 1896.

U.S. President McKinley's decree of December 21, 1898, asserting American military sovereignty over the Philippines even before the Senate ratified the Treaty of Paris — a direct refusal to recognize the already-declared Philippine Republic, and the immediate lead-up to the Philippine-American War.
A national holiday observed every November 30, commemorating Andrés Bonifacio's birth (1863) and honoring his life and sacrifice as the Father of the Philippine Revolution.

A local village headman, drawn from the native principalia, responsible for tribute collection, census registration, cédulas, and organizing forced labor — the position Francisco Dagohoy held before leading his rebellion.
A compulsory residence certificate and head-tax receipt symbolizing submission to Spanish rule; tearing it up (as at the Cry of Pugad Lawin) was a direct declaration of defiance.
Spanish colonial society was organized into layers, roughly from most to least privileged.

sub-content.meaning: Spaniards born in Spain; held the highest political and religious power.
People of pure Spanish descent born in the Philippines; historically the only group the term "Filipino" applied to.
The educated class of native, mestizo, and elite Filipino students (often university- or Europe-trained) who reclaimed the word "Filipino" for all Filipinos and pushed for reform.
People of mixed Spanish-native or Chinese-native ancestry, often wealthy through trade, but without real political power.
The local native elite who held town offices (like cabeza de barangay); respected locally, but mainly served as go-betweens who collected taxes and organized labor for Spain.
The Indigenous Filipino majority, at the bottom of this system; the group most heavily burdened by tribute taxes and forced labor.

content.meaning: The conservative reformist group formed by Mabini and others after La Liga Filipina's 1893 dissolution, to keep funding La Solidaridad. Its members chose to keep pursuing peaceful, legal reform, while radicals like Jose Dizon left to join the Katipunan instead.
The government post Bonifacio was elected to at the Tejeros Convention, before Daniel Tirona's public insult over his lack of a law degree triggered Bonifacio's annulment of the entire election.
A nature spirit from pre-colonial Visayan folklore, featured in local creation legends and animist spiritual traditions.

Rizal's second novel (Ghent, September 18, 1891), dedicated to the memory of the Gomburza martyrs. A darker sequel to Noli Me Tángere, it warns that an unguided, vengeful revolution risks replacing foreign oppressors with native tyrants — while still fueling the push toward armed struggle.

The Spanish land-and-labor system: native populations reorganized into towns (reducciones) under an encomendero, who collected tribute and forced labor (polo) in exchange for (nominal) protection and religious instruction. Became highly abusive in practice.
The Spanish officials or private agents granted an encomienda; entitled to collect tribute and demand labor from the population under their control.
The native mayor of a town, drawn from the local elite; responsible for civil administration, policing, and municipal budgets.
The highest-ranking Spanish authority in the Philippines, representing the Crown directly, with sweeping executive, military, and judicial power.

A Jesuit appointed to administer a parish under royal patronage, acting as both spiritual guide and civil agent of the Crown — a dual role that often bred local resentment, as with Father Gaspar Morales.
The Katipunan's clandestine newspaper ("Freedom"); one issue published March 1896, falsely datelined "Yokohama" to mislead Spanish authorities — a powerful spark for rapid membership growth.

Emilio Jacinto's official moral and civic primer for the Katipunan, containing fourteen propositions on human equality, honor, charity, and self-actualization; adopted by Bonifacio as the society's official teaching, replacing his own Dekalogo.

The sovereign nation imagined by Bonifacio and Jacinto, encompassing the entire archipelago — a term meant to include Visayans, Ilocanos, Pampangos, and all other peoples as equal "children of the nation," bypassing colonial and racial classifications.

The revolutionary secret society, full name Kataas-taasan, Kagalang-galangang Katipunan ng mga Anak ng Bayan, founded July 7, 1892, in Tondo. Patterned its structure and initiation rites on Freemasonry. On August 24, 1896, it transformed from a clandestine network into an open, de facto national government, declaring a nationwide armed revolution.
The supreme ruler of the Spanish Empire; issued the royal charters and instructions that directed colonization and established sovereignty over territories like the Kingdom of New Castile.

content.term: Kingdom of New Castile (El Reyno de Nueva Castilla)
content.meaning: The official name King Philip II gave the Philippine archipelago as a Spanish crown realm (a reyno, not a mere colony), with Manila designated as its capital — formalized on the ground June 24, 1571.

Rizal's peaceful, non-violent mutual-aid society, founded July 3, 1892, aiming to unite the archipelago, provide mutual protection, and pursue reform. Suspended after Rizal's arrest, revived in April 1893, and dissolved in October 1893 due to the ideological split between wealthy reformists and working-class radicals.

The fortnightly reformist newspaper (Barcelona, Feb. 1889–Nov. 1895) at the heart of the Propaganda Movement, publishing critiques of colonial abuse and pushing for Filipino representation in the Spanish Cortes.

The Cavite Katipunan council under Emilio Aguinaldo, named for his Katipunan name (itself drawn from Kawit's patron saint). Based in Kawit, expanding toward southern Manila, and presided over on paper by Baldomero Aguinaldo. Pursued a distinct republican model that ultimately bypassed Bonifacio's authority.
The Cavite Katipunan council loyal to Bonifacio's central authority, covering Noveleta, San Francisco de Malabon, and territory toward Batangas.
Bonifacio's late-March 1897 attempt to keep a separate revolutionary government and command structure alive after annulling the Tejeros Convention's results.

The traditional pre-colonial Filipino dwelling: lightweight, bamboo-framed, and nipa-thatched — practical and quick to build, but highly flammable, as shown catastrophically at Cebu on April 27, 1565.

Rizal's first novel (Berlin, March 1887); a critique of friar abuse and colonial stagnation that was quickly banned — which only fueled its influence in building a unified Filipino national consciousness.
The truce signed December 14, 1897, between Aguinaldo's forces and Spain: Spain paid indemnity, and Aguinaldo's cabinet went into voluntary exile in Hong Kong.
The colonial system (established 1580) requiring native men aged 16–60 to perform 40 days of unpaid labor a year (reduced to 15 in 1884) — a major cause of labor shortages, starvation, and revolt.
The designation for how Aguinaldo was elected President at the Tejeros Convention despite not being physically present for the vote.
A national holiday observed every December 30, honoring Rizal's life, literature, and execution — the moment that became the definitive rallying point for the armed revolution.
The Spanish colonial high court, managing justice and administrative oversight, and serving as a check on colonial officials.
The pre-colonial blood-compact covenant of friendship and alliance, sealed by mixing a drop of each leader's blood into shared water or wine.

content.term: Sigaw ng Pugad Lawin (Cry of Pugad Lawin)
content.meaning: The August 23, 1896 mass tearing of cédulas by the Katipuneros, marking their formal break from Spain; also called the "Cry of Balintawak," depending on the historical account.

The Katipunan's early, cautious recruitment system, where each member enlisted only two others who never learned each other's identities — very secure, but too slow, and abandoned for open recruitment in October 1892.

The March 22, 1897 meeting in Cavite, originally called to plan provincial defense, that instead elected a new revolutionary government — bypassing the Katipunan's Supreme Council and triggering a permanent leadership fracture.

A group of thirteen prominent Filipino patriots—consisting of Freemasons and members of Dr. José Rizal’s reformist La Liga Filipina—who were publicly executed by firing squad at Bagumbayan Field (now Luneta Park) on January 11, 1897, on charges of treason and sedition. Following the unmasking of the Katipunan in August 1896 by Father Mariano Gil and the colonial Cuerpo de Vigilancia, Spanish authorities launched a campaign of mass arrests, utilizing torture to extract names and confessions. Although several of the condemned men were peaceful, moderate reformists who had explicitly refused to fund or support Andrés Bonifacio's armed revolutionary path, the colonial administration labeled all Freemasons and Liga members as dangerous subversives, sentencing them to death in a bid to crush the uprising. The thirteen executed martyrs were:

sub-content.meaning: An insulare Mason and master of the second Filipino lodge, Logia Balagtas No. 149, who joined La Liga Filipina at its founding beside his father Ambrosio.
A legal advocate and reformist writer who served as the copyist mentor to a young Apolinario Mabini and championed the Grand Regional Council of Masons.
Founder of Logia Walana No. 158 and a key figure in La Liga Filipina, whose eighteen-year-old daughter Rosario was historically celebrated as the first female initiate in Philippine Masonry.
A reformist merchant from Capiz, close friend of Apolinario Mabini, and the elected president of the resurrected La Liga Filipina in April 1893.
A merchant, co-founder of the Katipunan, master of Logia Taliba, and maternal uncle to Emilio Jacinto.
A second lieutenant in the Spanish infantry who acted as a secret fundraiser and collector for the Katipunan.
A corporal in the Spanish army infantry who secretly worked as a Katipunan recruiter and officer in Bulacan.

A wealthy creole government adviser who refused to support the Katipunan’s radical agenda, but was tragically implicated when Bonifacio drew up a fake KKK membership list containing his name to force wealthy elites to support the cause.
Master of Logia Modestia and owner of Bazaar El Cisne, who secretly sold the printing press used by Jacinto and Bonifacio to publish the clandestine newspaper Kalayaan.
A port office clerk and Katipunan member who famously apologized to Emilio Aguinaldo to resolve an intense duel of honor.
An Albay-born reformist and abaca plantation heir educated at a Naga seminary, who was active in the Spanish Propaganda Movement.
A clerk and active Katipunero who established the Balangay Gitna chapter in his birthplace of Tondo.
A port clerk, Katipunan Supreme Council member under Bonifacio, and head of the Ilog Pasig council in Binondo.

content.meaning: The December 10, 1898 agreement ending the Spanish-American War: Spain ceded the Philippines, Guam, and Puerto Rico to the U.S. for $20 million, without any Filipino representation at the table.
The resented colonial tax on Filipinos aged 19–60 (1565–1884), often collected through force; its abusive collection was a major catalyst for over 200 local uprisings.
"One is worth all" — the Latin motto of La Liga Filipina, expressing the principle that collective strength and mutual defense outweigh individual self-interest.
